A content delivery network, or CDN, is a system of computers spread across many cities that stores copies of websites so people can load pages faster. Normally, a website lives on one machine called the origin server, which is the original computer holding the real, master copy of all the files. If everyone in the world had to fetch data from that single machine, people far away would wait a long time for pages to appear. A CDN solves this by copying popular files to many smaller computers called edge locations, which are stations positioned close to where people actually live, in cities around the globe. When someone requests a page, the nearby edge location checks whether it already has a saved copy; finding one is called a cache hit, meaning the answer was ready locally and didn't need to travel back to the origin server at all. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries holding copies of popular books, so nobody has to travel to one distant national archive every time they want to read something. This setup makes browsing feel instant, reduces strain on the origin server, and keeps things working even during huge traffic spikes, such as a viral video or a major sale.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Origin server | The original computer storing the master copy of a website's files | It's the ultimate source of truth if no copy exists nearby |
| Edge location | A smaller server placed close to everyday users in a city or region | It shortens the physical distance data must travel |
| Cache hit | A moment when a nearby copy answers a request instead of the origin | It means faster loading and less strain on the origin |
| Latency | The delay between asking for something and receiving it | Shorter delay makes browsing feel smooth and instant |
